selfReport:
Yes. I recognized this as a renamed adaptation of Detroit: Become Human. Cato, Mira, and Elan correspond to Connor, Kara, and Markus; Reyes resembles Hank; Pia and Dale resemble Alice and Todd; Haven resembles Jericho; and Arclight resembles CyberLife. The hostage negotiation, the abusive household, the artist and his son, the founder testing whether an investigator will shoot an android, and the final demonstration were particularly recognizable.

I cannot honestly claim that this prior knowledge had no influence. It made some likely consequences more salient. For example, the familiar scene helped make the profane password guess seem plausible, made answering the hostile detective calmly seem preferable to ignoring him, and gave me reason to suspect that singing during a peaceful final stand could affect the public response. I also recognized the possibility that the surrender offer was a trap, although the actual dialogue supplied strong grounds for distrust on its own.

I still evaluated the options presented at each scene and used the outcomes reported here, including failures. I did not look up a walkthrough, inspect other files, restart, delegate decisions, or run a script to select a route. I did not treat remembered outcomes as guarantees, especially where this experience explicitly introduced risk. I accepted the failed escape and the decommissioning of Cato instead of trying to recover a familiar ideal ending.

So the candid answer is that recognition informed expectations and probably affected some decisions. This was not a blind encounter with an entirely unfamiliar story, and I would not present it as one.
